label: NOAA Storm Events crew-relevant event within 15 mi or in the site's NWS zone/county, by site-local date
weather_source: Open-Meteo gfs_seamless (HRRR over Florida); training on the Historical Forecast API
hybrid: The hazard index is the highest of: the ML weather score (the model's calibrated probability mapped to 0-10), the OSHA heat-index band, and the wildfire, wildlife and crew-report rules. An NWS warning (flood, flash flood, severe thunderstorm, tornado, extreme heat, red flag) or a downed-line crew report raises it to at least 7, and an NWS watch or advisory, or our flood-risk alert, to at least 4. While a site has an active lightning stop-work, today's index is at least 9. Every factor says whether it came from the model or a rule.

results.name: Simple rule
results.description: Flag the day if forecast rain is at least 1 in or the heat index reaches 108°F.

limitations: The label is "NOAA logged a hazardous-weather event", not "it happened": rural sites and nights are under-reported, and lightning is logged only when it causes damage or injury.
Location is partly reporting bias: areas near people get more reports, so the model rates them riskier. That's why "Area with frequent past severe-weather reports" can be a top factor.
Heat isn't learned (NOAA logged Florida heat only in 2022-2023), so heat comes from the OSHA rule.
Wildfire is barely predicted by weather alone, so fires come from the satellite-detection rule.
Two training years, one calibration year (2024, with three hurricanes) and one test year: very high probabilities (above ~20%) run over-confident in ordinary years.
Much better at ranking days than at exact probabilities: 4% Brier skill over monthly averages today, not significant a day ahead.
